_activity: Review Bowl, short in-game questions: civic principles (Civic Principles card, word for word) and the Civic Literacy Essay (June 2026 exam wording)
_licence: ORIGINAL. Principle names and definitions from skills/unit0-print/build_civic_principles_card.py (BK 2026-09-26). CLE task words from the June 2026 Regents (ushg62026exam.pdf, Part III). One quotation: the Declaration of Independence, public domain.
_units: unit = the earliest unit that teaches it: 11.1+ means from 11.1 on; 11.2 means switch on when 11.2 opens (Thu 10/1).

items.stem: “No one is above the law, not even the people who make it.” Which principle is this?
hints: Think about Magna Carta: even the king had to follow the rules.
The principle has the word “law” in its name.
items.reason: Rule of Law: the law binds everyone, including the people who make it.

items.stem: “Government can only do what the Constitution allows.” Which principle is this?
hints: This principle puts a cap on government.
Look for the word that means “capped.”
items.reason: Limited Government: the Constitution sets the boundaries, and government stays inside them.

items.stem: Power is split among three branches: one makes laws, one carries them out, one judges them. Which principle is this?
hints: The key word is “split,” with each branch doing its own job.
It's not about branches blocking each other. That's a different principle.
items.reason: Separation of Powers: three branches, three different jobs.

items.stem: The president vetoes a bill, and Congress overrides the veto. Which principle is at work?
hints: One branch blocks another, and then it gets blocked back.
Look for the principle about branches limiting each other.
items.reason: Checks and Balances: each branch can block or limit the others. A veto and an override are both checks.

items.stem: Power is divided between the national government and the states. Which principle is this?
hints: This split isn't between branches. It's between levels of government.
Think: the nation versus a state.
items.reason: Federalism: power is shared between the nation and the states. When they clash, valid federal law wins.

items.stem: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Supreme Court strikes down part of a law passed by Congress. Which power does the Court claim?
hints: The Court is deciding whether a law fits the Constitution.
The principle has “judicial” (courts) in its name.
items.reason: Judicial Review: courts can strike down a law that breaks the Constitution. Marbury is where the Supreme Court claimed it.

items.stem: The Declaration says governments get “their just powers from the consent of the governed.” Which principle is this?
hints: Where does this line say government's power comes from?
Consent of the governed sits inside one principle on your card.
items.reason: Popular Sovereignty: government's power comes from the people, and it rules only with their agreement.
items.citation: Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776 (National Archives transcription)

items.stem: Every person is born with rights (life, liberty, property) that government exists to protect. Which principle is this?
hints: The key words are “born with.”
These rights come from being human, not from a government.
items.reason: Natural Rights: you're born with them, and government exists to protect them.

items.stem: The people elect officials to make decisions for them. Which principle is this?
hints: The key word is “elect.”
A representative is someone chosen to speak for you.
items.reason: Representative Government: voters choose officials to decide for them.

items.stem: The Stamp Act Congress (1765) says only the colonies' own elected assemblies can tax them. Which principle are they claiming?
hints: Who do the colonists say gets to tax them?
The key word is “elected.”
items.reason: Representative Government: no tax without lawmakers the people elected. That's “no taxation without representation.”

items.stem: Freedoms government can't take away, like speech, religion, press and assembly. Which principle is this?
hints: Think of the First Amendment.
These are also called civil liberties.
items.reason: Individual Rights (civil liberties): speech, religion, press and assembly, protected in the Bill of Rights.

items.stem: The Sedition Act of 1798 made it a crime to publish false or malicious writing against the government. Which principle is most at stake?
hints: What freedom does a newspaper editor need?
Think of the First Amendment: speech and press.
items.reason: Individual Rights (civil liberties): freedom of speech and press. The Sedition Act tested them seven years after the Bill of Rights.

items.stem: Someone is arrested and held for months with no trial. Which principle is at stake?
hints: What does government owe you before it takes away your liberty?
The principle is about fair steps.
items.reason: Due Process: government must follow fair steps, like a trial, before it takes your liberty.

items.stem: A law treats one group of people differently, or shuts them out. Which principle is at stake?
hints: The key word is “equally.”
Which principle says the law must treat people the same?
items.reason: Equal Protection: the law must treat people equally. It comes into its own with the 14th Amendment in 11.4.

items.stem: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Maryland tries to tax the national bank, and the Supreme Court says it can't. Which principle decides the case?
hints: It's a state against the national government.
When they clash, valid federal law wins.
items.reason: Federalism: the nation and the states share power, and when they clash, valid federal law wins.

items.stem: On the Civic Literacy Essay, “describe the historical circumstances” asks for which skill?
hints: Circumstances means what was going on around the issue.
It's the skill you practice in every CONTEXT CHECK.
items.reason: Historical Context: what was happening, and what led to the issue, before you argue about it.

items.stem: The Civic Literacy Essay says to use information from at least how many documents?
hints: It's more than half of the six documents.
More than three, fewer than six.
items.reason: At least four. Using all six is fine, but four is the floor.

items.stem: The Civic Literacy Essay asks you to explain at least how many efforts to address the issue?
hints: An effort is something people or a government did about the issue.
More than one, fewer than three.
items.reason: At least two efforts, by individuals, groups or governments.

items.stem: What counts as outside information on the Civic Literacy Essay?

options.1: A quote copied from one of the documents
options.3: A relevant fact you know that isn't in any of the documents
options.4: A summary of the historical context paragraph

hints: “Outside” means outside the documents.
It has to be relevant, and it has to be a fact you bring.
items.reason: Outside information is relevant history you bring from outside the documents. The exam and your gauge use the same name.

items.stem: On the Civic Literacy Essay, “discuss the impact of the efforts” asks you to…

options.2: Tell what changed because of the efforts, using facts and reasoning

hints: “Impact” means effect.
Discuss means using facts, reasoning and argument.
items.reason: Discuss the impact: what changed for the country or its people because of the efforts, backed with facts and reasoning.

items.stem: The June 2026 Civic Literacy Essay was about creating a stronger national government. Which plan of government showed the problem it was meant to fix?
hints: Which plan built a national government too weak to tax?
It came before the Constitution, in 1781.
items.reason: The Articles of Confederation built a government too weak to tax or enforce its laws. The Constitution replaced it.
